title: Decimals: The Space Between Whole Numbers

blocks.title: 1. The Core Concept: Dividing the Whole
blocks.content: Whole numbers are like stepping stones: 1, 2, 3, 4... But what about the mud between the stones? **Decimals** fill in those gaps. The number 3.7 sits between 3 and 4, exactly 7 tenths of the way across. Every digit after the decimal point represents a smaller and smaller fraction: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. They let you measure things with razor-sharp precision.

blocks.title: 2. The Rules: Place Value After the Point
blocks.content:
After the decimal point, each column is 10x smaller:

• 1st place: **Tenths** (0.1)
• 2nd place: **Hundredths** (0.01)
• 3rd place: **Thousandths** (0.001)

So 0.253 means 2 tenths + 5 hundredths + 3 thousandths.

**Key Rule:** When comparing decimals, pad with trailing zeros first! 0.5 is the SAME as 0.500.

blocks.title: 3. Step-by-Step: Multiplying Decimals
blocks.content:
To multiply decimals (e.g., 2.4 x 1.3):

1. **Ignore the decimal points** and multiply as whole numbers: 24 x 13 = 312.
2. **Count decimal places** in the original numbers: 2.4 has 1, and 1.3 has 1. Total = 2.
3. **Place the decimal point** in your answer 2 places from the right: 3.12.

This trick works every single time!

blocks.title: 4. Worked Example: Dividing Decimals
blocks.content:
Calculate 7.2 / 0.4.

**Step 1:** Make the divisor a whole number. Multiply both by 10: 72 / 4.
**Step 2:** Now it's a simple division: 72 / 4 = 18.

**Final Answer: 7.2 / 0.4 = 18.**

(The trick: always multiply both numbers by 10 or 100 until the divisor has no decimal point.)

blocks.title: 5. Common Pitfalls
blocks.content: The most devastating mistake: when multiplying 0.2 x 0.3, students often write 0.6 instead of 0.06. Count the decimal places: 0.2 has 1 place, 0.3 has 1 place. Total = 2 places. So 2 x 3 = 6, and you need 2 decimal places: 0.06. If you don't count places correctly, your answer will be 10x or 100x off!
